glossary.def: The basic Roman heavy-infantry formation. Polybius' manipular legion had 4,200 infantry (1,200 velites, 1,200 hastati, 1,200 principes, 600 triarii) and 300 cavalry; the late Republican and imperial legion c. 4,800-5,500 men in 10 cohorts (the first double-strength from the later 1st century AD) with 120 cavalry, numbered and named (Legio X Fretensis). Under the empire about 25-33 legions formed the citizen core of the army; late Roman legions were much smaller units of 1,000-3,000.

Tactical unit of two centuries (120 men for hastati and principes, 60 for triarii) in the middle Republican legion, deployed in a checkerboard (quincunx) of three lines allowing relief and flexibility; adopted, by tradition, during the Samnite Wars.

Unit of three maniples (c. 480 men in six centuries of 80) which became the main tactical subdivision of the legion by the late 2nd century BC; also the standard unit of auxiliary infantry (cohors quingenaria of c. 480 or milliaria of c. 800) and of the Praetorian, urban and vigiles units.
Company of the legion commanded by a centurion: 80 men (ten contubernia) under the empire, despite the name.
Squad of eight legionaries sharing a tent (papilio) and a mule, the smallest unit of the legion; ten made a century.
First line of the manipular legion: younger men with scutum, gladius and two pila.
Second line of the manipular legion: men in their prime, equipped like the hastati.
Third line of the manipular legion: veterans with thrusting spears, kneeling in reserve; 'res ad triarios rediit' meant a desperate situation.
Light-armed skirmishers of the manipular legion, the youngest and poorest, with javelins and small round shields; abolished in the reforms of the later 2nd century BC.

Modern label for changes attributed to Marius c. 107-101 BC: enrolling the capite censi as volunteers, cohort organization, the eagle as sole legionary standard, the improved pilum and soldiers carrying their own kit ('Marius' mules'). Many changes were gradual (cohorts appear earlier; property qualifications had already fallen), and the link between volunteer armies and client armies loyal to generals is debated.

Officer commanding a century, the professional backbone of the legion: about 60 per legion, graded by cohort and seniority, culminating in the primus pilus. Paid many times a legionary's salary; promotion came from the ranks or by direct equestrian commission.

Senior centurion of the first cohort, commanding its first century and the legion's eagle; on retirement entitled to equestrian rank and a large bonus, often going on to praefectus castrorum or procuratorships.
Deputy to a centurion (or decurion), chosen by him, standing at the rear of the century.
Standard-bearer of a century, also responsible for the unit's savings bank.

The silver (later gold) eagle standard of a legion, carried by the aquilifer and kept in the shrine of the headquarters; its loss was the ultimate disgrace (the eagles of Carrhae, recovered 20 BC; the three of Varus, two recovered in AD 15-16 and 41).

(1) In the Republic, an allied contingent (ala sociorum) roughly equivalent to a legion, posted on the wings. (2) Under the empire, an auxiliary cavalry regiment of c. 500 (quingenaria, 16 turmae) or 1,000 (milliaria, 24 turmae), commanded by an equestrian prefect; the ala milliaria command was the summit of the equestrian militiae.

Non-citizen regiments (alae of cavalry, cohorts of infantry, mixed cohortes equitatae) recruited from provincials and formally organized under Augustus, roughly matching the legions in number; soldiers received citizenship on discharge after 25 years (recorded on diplomas) until the Constitutio Antoniniana. Ethnic names (Batavi, Tungri, Thracians) reflect origin, not later recruitment.
Auxiliary cohort with an attached cavalry element (c. 120 or 240 horse), well suited to frontier policing.

Generic term for a military unit; specifically irregular ethnic units of the 2nd-3rd centuries (numeri Brittonum, Palmyrene archers, Moorish cavalry) outside the standard auxilia. In late antiquity a standard term for a regiment (arithmos in Greek).

Detachment drawn from one or more legions or auxiliary units and sent on campaign under a vexillum flag, increasingly common from the 2nd century; in the late army, vexillationes were the cavalry regiments of the field armies.
Commander of a turma (about 30 troopers) in an auxiliary ala or of the legionary cavalry.
Third in command of a legion, usually an ex-primus pilus, responsible for the fortress, engineering, supplies and training.

The emperor's guard, formed by Augustus from the Republican commander's cohors praetoria: nine (later ten to sixteen) cohorts of 500-1,000 Italians with higher pay and 16-year service, concentrated in the Castra Praetoria by Sejanus (c. AD 23). Kingmakers (Claudius 41, Otho 69, the auction of 193); Severus replaced it with provincial legionaries (193); disbanded by Constantine after the Milvian Bridge (312).
Police force of Rome (three, later four cohorts) under the urban prefect, created by Augustus; detachments at Lugdunum (guarding the mint) and Carthage.
Rome's fire brigade and night watch, 7 cohorts of freedmen (later freeborn) under the praefectus vigilum, from AD 6, with buckets, pumps, axes and blankets.

The imperial navy: praetorian fleets at Misenum and Ravenna, provincial fleets (classis Britannica, Germanica on the Rhine, Pannonica and Moesica on the Danube, Alexandrina, Syriaca, Pontica), manned by provincials on 26-year service. In the Republic the fleets of the Punic Wars were built ad hoc (Rome reportedly built 100 quinqueremes in 60 days in 261 BC).

Boarding bridge with a spike used by the Roman fleet in the First Punic War (Mylae 260, Ecnomus 256), turning sea battles into infantry fights; probably abandoned because it made ships unstable in storms.

A fortified camp. On campaign legions built marching camps every night to a standard plan (Polybius 6.27-42; Pseudo-Hyginus). Permanent fortresses (castra stativa) of c. 20 ha for a legion, with principia, praetorium, barracks, granaries and baths, became the nuclei of many cities (Chester, York, Vienna, León).
Formation in which soldiers locked shields overhead and around to approach walls under missile fire, shown on Trajan's and Marcus' columns.
Heavy javelin with a long iron shank designed to bend or penetrate shields, thrown before the charge; two were carried by Republican legionaries.
The short stabbing sword (gladius Hispaniensis, adopted from Iberians in the 3rd century BC; later Mainz and Pompeii types). Replaced in the 3rd century AD by the longer spatha.
Legionary shield: curved oval in the Republic (the Fayum example), curved rectangular under the early empire, replaced by flat oval shields in the 3rd century.
Modern name for the articulated iron plate cuirass of legionaries from the early 1st to the 3rd century AD (Kalkriese, Corbridge and Newstead types); coexisted with mail (lorica hamata) and scale.

Torsion artillery powered by twisted sinew skeins: stone throwers (ballistae) and bolt shooters (catapultae, scorpiones); each imperial legion had about 60 cart-mounted carroballistae and 10 stone throwers according to Vegetius. The one-armed onager appears in the 4th century.
One-armed torsion stone thrower named after its 'kick', described by Ammianus (23.4).

Siege lines around a besieged place, with an outer contravallation against relief forces, as at Alesia (52 BC: c. 15 and 21 km of works), Numantia (134-133) and Masada (73/74, the circumvallation and ramp still visible).

Procession of a victorious general with his army, captives and spoils from the Campus Martius to the Capitol, where he sacrificed to Jupiter; voted by the Senate for a major victory by a magistrate with imperium (in theory 5,000 enemies killed). Some 320 triumphs in the Fasti; after 19 BC reserved for the imperial family, others receiving ornamenta triumphalia.
Lesser triumph on foot or horseback, wreathed in myrtle, for victories over unworthy enemies (slaves, pirates) or without full war; Crassus' ovation after Spartacus (71 BC).

Arms stripped by a Roman commander from an enemy commander killed in single combat, dedicated to Jupiter Feretrius; only three cases (Romulus, Cossus, Marcellus in 222 BC). Augustus blocked Crassus' claim (29 BC) by ruling that Cossus had been consul.
Punishment of a cowardly unit by executing every tenth man chosen by lot, the others beaten by their comrades; rare (Crassus against Spartacus, Antony in 36 BC).
Oath sworn by soldiers on enlistment to their commander, later to the emperor, renewed annually.

Conscription of citizens for the legions, held by consuls each year in the Republic from the assidui; under the empire mostly volunteers, with conscription in emergencies (AD 6 and 9) and in late antiquity a levy of recruits from landowners (praebitio tironum) commutable into gold.
Discharge after full service with privileges and a gratuity: from AD 6 the aerarium militare paid legionary veterans 12,000 sesterces (Augustus), later 20,000 (Caracalla).

Pair of bronze tablets certifying the grant of citizenship and conubium (right of marriage) to discharged auxiliaries and sailors, copied from the master list on the Capitol; over 1,000 known, dating from Claudius to c. 300, invaluable for unit locations.
Cash gift to soldiers on an emperor's accession or other occasions; Claudius gave the Praetorians 15,000 sesterces each (41), Marcus and Lucius 20,000 (161).

Soldiers' pay, introduced traditionally during the siege of Veii (406-396 BC). Annual legionary pay: c. 112.5 denarii in the mid-Republic (Polybius' 2 obols a day), 225 under Caesar, 300 under Domitian, 450 under Severus, 675 or 750 under Caracalla; deductions for food and kit. In late antiquity pay was largely in kind (annona) plus gold donatives. Also the fixed tribute of some provinces.
Veterans recalled to service, often as specialists or junior officers; Praetorian evocati served the emperor in administrative roles.

Originally a road or path, later the fortified frontier zone of the empire with its roads, forts and watchtowers: the Upper German-Raetian limes (palisade and wall, 550 km), Hadrian's Wall, the Antonine Wall, the Danube and Euphrates frontiers, the fossatum Africae. Modern debate concerns whether frontiers were defensive lines (Luttwak's 'grand strategy') or zones of control and exchange (Isaac, Whittaker).

Late Roman frontier troops (also ripenses on rivers) under duces, distinguished from the field armies by Constantine's time; given land and lower status, often stereotyped as peasant militia, though they remained real soldiers into the 6th century. Justinian reconstituted them in Africa (534).

Soldiers of the mobile field armies (comitatus) created by Diocletian and Constantine, under magistri militum; better paid and privileged over the limitanei. The Notitia shows regional field armies (Gaul, Illyricum, Thrace, Oriens) and two praesental armies in the East.
The senior regiments of the field armies, originally attached to the emperor's person; higher pay and precedence than comitatenses.
Frontier units transferred to the field armies, ranking below comitatenses; a symptom of the 4th-5th century drain on frontier forces.

Allies bound by treaty (foedus). In the 4th-5th centuries, barbarian groups settled or subsidized under their own leaders to fight for Rome (the Goths of 382, the Visigoths in Aquitaine 418); in the 6th century, a regular corps of mixed recruitment under Roman officers.
Private armed retainers of generals and magnates, named after the hard-tack (bucellatum) they were fed; Belisarius had up to 7,000. Took an oath to the emperor as well as their patron.
Barbarian settlers given land in Gaul and Italy in return for hereditary military service, attested from the Tetrarchy (Panegyric of 297) and in the Notitia's praefecti laetorum.

Heavily armoured cavalry with horse armour, modelled on Sarmatian and Parthian/Sasanian lancers; Roman units from Hadrian (ala I Gallorum et Pannoniorum catafractaria), expanded in the 3rd-4th centuries; clibanarii ('oven men') was a related term for fully enclosed riders.

Some 35 state arms factories listed in the Notitia under the magister officiorum (shields at Augustodunum, armour at Antioch, artillery at Augustodunum and Treveri), staffed by hereditary fabricenses.

Imperial guard cavalry regiments created by Constantine (each c. 500 men), under the magister officiorum, largely Germanic in the 4th century; by the 6th century a showpiece, displaced by the excubitors.
Palace guard of 300 founded by Leo I (c. 460), often Isaurian; their commander (comes excubitorum) became a kingmaker: Justin I and Tiberius II rose from that post.
Corps of officer-cadets attached to the emperor from the mid-3rd century, a route to command (Diocletian and Ammianus served as protectores).

College of priests (3, later 9 from 300 BC, 15 under Sulla, 16 under Caesar) supervising state cult, sacred law, the calendar and intercalation, burial and adoption law, and keeping the annual tablet of events (tabula, later the Annales maximi in 80 books). Members were co-opted, then elected by 17 tribes from 104 BC.
Priest of a single god: three major flamines (Dialis of Jupiter, Martialis, Quirinalis), patrician, and twelve minor; later flamines of deified emperors in Rome and the provinces.

Priest of Jupiter, bound by archaic taboos (no touching iron, horses or ivy, could not spend a night away from Rome or see an army), which made the post hard to fill; vacant from 87 BC (the young Caesar was designated but never inaugurated) to 11 BC.
'King of sacred rites', a patrician priest who inherited the religious functions of the kings, barred from political office; outranked even the pontifex maximus in the order of precedence.
Member of the college of augurs (9 from 300 BC, 15 under Sulla) who interpreted signs of divine will (auspices) and could declare acts vitiated; inaugurated templa. Cicero was an augur from 53 BC.

Etruscan diviner who read the entrails of sacrificial animals (especially the liver: the Piacenza bronze liver), lightning and prodigies; consulted by the Senate, not a Roman priesthood. Claudius created an ordo of 60 haruspices; Spurinna warned Caesar of the Ides of March.

Six priestesses of Vesta, chosen as girls aged 6-10 for 30 years of chastity, guarding the eternal fire and sacred objects (including the Palladium) in the temple of Vesta. Unchastity was punished by burial alive (some ten cases, e.g. 216 and 114-113 BC). Disbanded under Theodosius (c. 394).

College (2, then 10 from 367 BC, 15 under Sulla) that kept and consulted the Sibylline Books when ordered by the Senate and oversaw foreign cults (Magna Mater, Apollo); organized the Secular Games of 17 BC.

Oracular books in Greek hexameters, by legend bought by Tarquin from the Cumaean Sibyl, consulted in crises; they prescribed new cults (the lectisternium of 399 BC, the Magna Mater in 205, burial alive of Greeks and Gauls in 228 and 216). Burned with the Capitol in 83 BC and reconstituted; destroyed by Stilicho c. 408.

College of 20 priests responsible for the rituals of treaties and declarations of war (rerum repetitio, throwing a spear into enemy territory, later into a column by the temple of Bellona), ensuring a 'just war'. Octavian revived the rite against Cleopatra (32 BC).
A war declared with the proper fetial forms after a demand for reparation, so assured of divine favour; a principle Cicero theorized (De officiis 1.36) and Augustine later Christianized.
Leaping priests of Mars (and Quirinus) who danced through the city in March and October with the sacred shields (ancilia), singing the archaic Carmen Saliare.

College of 12 priests of Dea Dia revived by Augustus; their inscribed records (Acta Fratrum Arvalium, 21 BC-AD 304) at the grove at La Magliana record sacrifices for the imperial house, the archaic Carmen Arvale, and dates of accessions.

Purificatory sacrifice (suovetaurilia: pig, sheep, bull) performed by a censor on the Campus Martius to close the census, then the five-year period between censuses; not every censorship ended in a lustrum.

Registration of citizens, their families and property by the censors, determining tribe, class, military liability and tax; returns were reported in totals (130,000 in 508 to 910,000 in 70 BC; 4,063,000 in 28 BC, see the debate on the change). Provincial censuses under Augustus (the census of Quirinius in Judaea, AD 6) assessed tribute; late Roman censuses assessed capitatio and iugatio.

(1) The calendar of days on which legal business was permitted (dies fasti) or forbidden (nefasti), with festivals and market days; published by Gnaeus Flavius in 304 BC, reformed by Caesar (the Julian calendar of 365.25 days, from 1 Jan 45 BC, after the 'year of confusion' of 445 days in 46). Painted and inscribed calendars survive (Fasti Antiates maiores, pre-Julian; Praenestini by Verrius Flaccus). (2) Lists of magistrates (fasti consulares) and triumphs (fasti triumphales), the backbone of Roman chronology, above all the Augustan Fasti Capitolini.

Note placed by the censors beside a citizen's name for moral or civic failings, with consequences such as expulsion from the Senate, loss of the public horse or transfer to an inferior tribe (aerarii).

The sacred boundary of the city, marked by stones, within which imperium militiae lapsed, armies could not enter (except for a triumph), burial was forbidden and the auspices were urban. Extended by Sulla, Claudius (49) and Vespasian; Aurelian's walls did not follow it.
Space inaugurated by augurs for taking auspices or holding meetings (the Senate had to meet in a templum, so the Curia was one); by extension a temple building (properly aedes).

Ritual by which a Roman commander vowed himself and the enemy army to the gods of the underworld and charged to his death, as the Decii Mures did at Veseris (340 BC) and Sentinum (295), and reportedly the grandson at Ausculum (279).
Ritual summoning of an enemy city's tutelary god to Rome with the promise of a new temple, as Camillus did with Juno Regina of Veii (396 BC); also reported for Carthage (146).

Greek-style feast in which images of gods were laid on couches before food, first ordered by the Sibylline Books in 399 BC during a pestilence, and on a grand scale for twelve gods in 217 after Trasimene.
Public prayer and thanksgiving at all temples, decreed by the Senate in crises or for victories; Caesar received unprecedented supplications of 15 (57 BC), 20 and 50 days.

Unnatural event (talking cattle, rains of blood or stones, lightning strikes, monstrous births) reported to the Senate as a sign that the pax deorum was broken, expiated on the advice of pontiffs, Sibylline Books or haruspices. Livy's annual prodigy lists and Obsequens preserve hundreds.
The 'peace of the gods', the right relationship between Rome and its gods maintained by correct ritual, whose breach was revealed by prodigies and defeats.

Annual rite of driving a nail into the wall of the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Ides of September, said to mark the years; in crises a dictator clavi figendi causa was appointed to perform it to avert plague (363, 331, 313?, 263 BC).
Italic vow dedicating everything born in a spring to the gods; children born then were sent out as adults to found new communities (Sabellian migrations). Rome vowed one in 217 BC (performed 195).

Worship of the emperor, his genius or numen, and deified predecessors (divi), with temples (Rome and Augustus at Pergamum and Ancyra, the altar of the Three Gauls at Lugdunum), provincial priesthoods and the Augustales; refusal to sacrifice became the test in persecutions.

Title of an emperor (or empress) deified by vote of the Senate after death (consecratio), with temple, flamen and cult: Julius Caesar (42 BC), Augustus, Claudius, Vespasian, Titus and most later emperors until Constantine (deified 337). Funeral eagles released from the pyre symbolized the ascent.
The divine guardian spirit of a man (and the paterfamilias); oaths by the emperor's genius and offerings to the genius Augusti were core acts of loyalty.

Household gods: Lares of the house and crossroads (Lares compitales, reorganized by Augustus with his genius in the 265 vici of Rome in 7 BC) and Penates of the storeroom; the public Penates were associated with Aeneas.

Phrygian mother goddess brought from Pessinus (or Pergamum) in 205/204 BC on Sibylline advice during the Hannibalic war, as a black stone; temple on the Palatine (191). Her castrated priests (galli) were foreigners, with Romans barred until Claudius.
The 'Unconquered Sun', elevated by Aurelian (274) with a temple, a college of pontifices Solis and games on 25 December; prominent on Constantine's coins until c. 325.

Persecution of Christians launched by Diocletian and Galerius with four edicts (Feb 303 to early 304): destruction of churches and scriptures, arrest of clergy, universal sacrifice. Enforced unevenly (lightly in Constantius' west, harshly in the east under Galerius and Maximinus) until Galerius' edict of toleration (311) and the settlement of 313.
Certificate that its holder had sacrificed to the gods before commissioners, required by Decius' edict of 249/250; some 46 survive on papyrus from Egypt, including one for a priestess of Petesouchos.

Conventional name for the agreement of Constantine and Licinius at Milan (Feb 313), known from Licinius' letter to the governor of Bithynia (Lactantius DMP 48; Eusebius HE 10.5), granting freedom of worship to all and restoring confiscated church property. Not an edict, nor issued at Milan.

Theology attributed to Arius of Alexandria (c. 318), that the Son was created and subordinate to the Father; condemned at Nicaea (325) but favoured in various forms (homoian) by Constantius II and Valens, and adopted by the Goths through Ulfilas, becoming the faith of most Germanic kingdoms until Reccared's conversion (587/589).

Creed of the Council of Nicaea (325) declaring the Son 'of the same substance' (homoousios) as the Father; reaffirmed and expanded at Constantinople (381) and made the test of orthodoxy by Theodosius' edict Cunctos populos (380).
Empire-wide council of bishops convened by the emperor: Nicaea (325), Constantinople (381), Ephesus (431), Chalcedon (451), Constantinople II (553); later councils continued (680-681, 787).

The Council of Chalcedon (451) defined Christ as one person 'in two natures'. Opponents (Miaphysites, called Monophysites by their enemies) held to 'one nature' after the union, dominant in Egypt, much of Syria and Armenia; repeated imperial compromises (Henotikon 482, Justinian's Three Chapters, Heraclius' Monoenergism and Monotheletism 638) failed to reunite the churches.

North African schism from 311 over bishops who had handed over scriptures in the persecution (traditores); the Donatist church rejected sacraments by such clergy, became the majority in Numidia, and was condemned by Constantine and repressed after the Conference of Carthage (411), with Augustine its chief opponent.

Title of the bishops of the major sees: Rome, Constantinople (second in rank by canon 3 of 381, equal privileges by canon 28 of Chalcedon, contested by Rome), Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem (from 451), the later 'pentarchy'.

Head of the Christian community of a city; after Constantine bishops gained judicial powers (episcopalis audientia), exemptions and wealth, and became civic leaders who negotiated with invaders (Leo with Attila in 452) and ran cities in the post-Roman West.

Bronze unit of account and coin. Originally a pound of bronze (aes grave, cast from c. 280 BC), reduced to sextantal (2 oz) around the introduction of the denarius c. 211 BC, uncial (1 oz) c. 141 and semuncial (lex Papiria, 91). Imperial as in copper, a quarter of a sestertius, 1/16 denarius.
Early Roman bronze money: aes rude (raw lumps), aes signatum (cast bars with designs, c. 300-250 BC) and aes grave (heavy cast round coins of the libral as and fractions, from c. 280 BC).

Rome's first silver coins, struck in the Greek standard from c. 310-300 BC for southern Italy, culminating in the quadrigatus (Janus and Jupiter in a quadriga) of the First and Second Punic Wars, replaced by the denarius.

Rome's main silver coin, introduced c. 211 BC (the date established from the hoard at Morgantina) at 1/72 pound (c. 4.5 g), reduced to 1/84 (c. 3.9 g) by the 190s-170s, tariffed at 10 asses then 16 (c. 141 BC). Nero reduced it to 1/96 pound and lowered fineness (64); progressive debasement from Marcus to Severus (c. 50% by 211), superseded by the antoninianus in the 240s. Diocletian's denarius communis was a unit of account.
Silver coin (c. 3.4 g) issued alongside the early denarius, valued at three-quarters of a denarius, probably for trade with Greek southern Italy; discontinued c. 170 BC and revived as the quinarius.
Silver half-denarius, struck intermittently from 211 BC, regularly from 101 BC (the lex Clodia) for Gallic trade.

Originally a small silver coin worth 2.5 asses (a quarter denarius); the standard unit of account in which large sums and fortunes were reckoned (HS). Augustus made it a large orichalcum (brass) coin worth 4 asses, the great medium of imperial portraiture; struck until the 260s.
Brass coin worth two asses (half a sestertius), distinguished from the as from Nero by the radiate crown on the emperor.

Gold coin worth 25 denarii, struck occasionally in the Republic (emergency issues of 211-209, Sulla, Pompey) and regularly from Caesar (c. 8 g, 1/40 pound); reduced to 1/45 (Nero), 1/50 (Caracalla), and unstable in the 3rd century; reset at 1/60 by Diocletian, replaced by the solidus.

Silver coin introduced by Caracalla in 215, a double denarius with radiate portrait but only about 1.5 times its silver; revived in 238, it collapsed under Gallienus to c. 2-5% silver with a surface wash. Aurelian's reformed radiate (274) bore XXI. Ancient name unknown.
High-purity silver coin (c. 3 g, 1/96 pound, c. 90% silver) introduced in Diocletian's reform of c. 294, intended to restore Neronian standards; issued only briefly in quantity.

Modern name for the large silver-washed bronze coin introduced in Diocletian's reform (c. 294, c. 10 g, GENIO POPVLI ROMANI), repeatedly reduced in the 4th century. Anastasius' reform of 498 created a new large copper follis of 40 nummi marked M, with denominations of 20 (K), 10 (I) and 5 (E).
Generic 'coin'; in late antiquity the smallest copper coin, of which the 5th-century West and East struck vast numbers of tiny pieces; the unit of the Anastasian follis system (40 nummi = 1 follis).

Gold coin introduced by Constantine (c. 309-312) at 72 to the pound (c. 4.5 g), kept stable for seven centuries as the 'dollar of the Middle Ages' (nomisma). Taxes, salaries and subsidies were reckoned in solidi and pounds of gold; the tremissis (one-third) and semissis (half) were fractions.
Gold third of a solidus, introduced c. 383; the main gold coin of the Germanic successor kingdoms.

Late Roman silver coins: the siliqua (1/24 of a solidus by value, c. 2-3 g, named from the carob seed weight) and the heavier miliarense (1/1000 of a pound of gold in theory). The Hoxne hoard (buried after 407) contained over 14,000 siliquae.
Heavy silver coin (c. 6.5 g, two grammata) introduced by Heraclius in 615 to pay the army, partly struck from church plate requisitioned for the Persian war; inscribed DEUS ADIUTA ROMANIS.

Greek unit of weight and money (Attic talent c. 26 kg = 6,000 drachmas, roughly 6,000 denarii), used for indemnities: Carthage paid 3,200 talents after 241 BC and 10,000 after 201; Antiochus III 15,000 at Apamea.

Roman pound of c. 327 g, divided into 12 unciae; coin standards were expressed as fractions of the pound (aureus 1/40, solidus 1/72), and large payments in pounds of gold (Rua's 350 lb a year, Attila's 2,100).
Dry measure of about 8.7 litres (c. 6.5 kg of wheat); a grain ration of 5 modii a month was standard for the frumentationes and soldiers.
Land measure of 28,800 square Roman feet (c. 0.25 ha), 'what a yoke of oxen could plough in a day'; colonists received 2 to 10 iugera in early colonies and Gracchan allotments up to 30.

Division of colonial or allotted land into square grids (centuriae, usually 20 x 20 actus, c. 710 m on a side, = 200 iugera) by surveyors (agrimensores), still visible in the Po valley, Tunisia and around Orange (whose marble cadastres survive).

Public land of the Roman people, mostly confiscated from defeated Italian communities, let to occupiers for a rent or leased by the censors; much was occupied by large holders. Tiberius Gracchus' law (133 BC) reclaimed holdings over 500 iugera (plus 250 per son) for allotment to the poor; the lex agraria of 111 privatized most of what remained.

The year's grain harvest, then the grain supply of Rome (and from 332 Constantinople) organized by the state, from Sicily, Sardinia, Africa and Egypt (Egypt alone sent some 20 million modii a year in the Augustan period, by Aurelius Victor's figure). In late antiquity also the system of taxes and rations in kind (annona militaris).
Requisition in kind for the army's food and fodder, regularized from the 3rd century into the annual assessment of the late Roman state (indiction); rations were later commuted into gold (adaeratio).

Distribution of grain to Roman citizens: subsidized by Gaius Gracchus' law (123 BC), free from Clodius' law (58 BC), with recipients fixed at about 200,000 by Augustus (2 BC) who received tickets (tesserae) for 5 modii monthly. Severus added oil, Aurelian bread, pork and wine.
Shippers who carried state grain under contract; from the 4th century a hereditary corporation compelled to serve, compensated with land and privileges.

Companies of equestrian contractors (societates publicanorum) who bid for state contracts: public works, army supply, mines and especially tax farming (the decuma of Asia let at Rome from 123 BC). Their extortion embittered the provinces (the 'Asian Vespers' of 88 BC); Caesar and Augustus curtailed tax farming of direct taxes.

Direct tax on Roman citizens' property, levied as a war tax until 167 BC, when the booty of Pydna allowed its suspension; thereafter tribute was paid by provincials (tributum soli on land, tributum capitis on persons), assessed by census.

Indirect taxes and revenues: customs dues (portoria, often 2.5% inland and 25% on the eastern frontier), rents from public land, mines, salt, the 5% manumission tax, and the 1% sales tax (centesima rerum venalium).

Tolls on goods crossing boundaries and harbours, collected at stations in regional districts (the quadragesima Galliarum, 2.5%; the 25% tetarte at the eastern frontier); the customs law of Asia (lex portorii Asiae, 62 AD inscription at Ephesus) survives.
Augustus' 5% inheritance tax on citizens (AD 6), with exemptions for close kin and small estates, earmarked for the aerarium militare; Caracalla doubled it to 10%.
State treasury in the temple of Saturn under the quaestors (under Augustus, praetors or prefects); progressively eclipsed by the emperor's fiscus.
Military treasury founded by Augustus in AD 6 with 170 million sesterces of his own money, funded by the 5% inheritance and 1% sales taxes, to pay veterans' discharge bonuses.
The emperor's treasury (originally 'basket'), receiving provincial revenues of imperial provinces and confiscations; by the 2nd century the main state treasury, managed by the a rationibus.
The emperor's private estates and their revenues, organized by Severus (managed by the comes rerum privatarum in late antiquity), swollen by confiscations and later by temple lands.

Diocletian's tax assessment system (from c. 287-297), measuring land in fiscal units (iuga, by quality and use) and labour in heads (capita), with an annual rate set by the praetorian prefects (indiction), collected in kind and later in gold; regional variations were large.

The annual tax assessment declared by the praetorian prefect; from 312 indictions ran in 15-year cycles beginning 1 September, becoming a standard dating system (Justinian made it obligatory in documents, 537).

Tax in gold and silver on merchants and craftsmen (including prostitutes), introduced by Constantine and levied every five years; notoriously oppressive (Zosimus); abolished by Anastasius in 498, who burned the records.
Commutation of taxes, rations or levies in kind into gold, increasingly common from the later 4th century as the solidus spread, notably for military rations and recruit levies.

Compulsory public services imposed on citizens and decurions (supplying transport, collecting taxes, maintaining roads or baths, funding games), the Roman counterpart of Greek liturgies; exemptions were a valuable privilege.

Three junior magistrates who supervised coinage in the Republic, increasingly signing coins with family types (from c. 140 BC); under Augustus their names disappeared (c. 4 BC) and the emperor controlled the mint.

The state transport and post system created by Augustus, with relay stations (mansiones, mutationes) and requisitioned animals and vehicles for officials with permits (diplomata, evectiones); burdensome to provincial communities, reformed by Nerva and Hadrian, run in late antiquity under the praetorian prefects and the agentes in rebus.

Originally the sphere of command assigned to a magistrate, then a territory under a Roman governor: Sicily (241 BC) and Sardinia-Corsica (238/227), the Spains (197), Macedonia and Africa (146), Asia (133), Narbonensis (c. 121), Cilicia, Bithynia, Cyrene, Syria and Crete in the 1st century BC. Some 45 under Hadrian, about 100 after Diocletian, around 120 by c. 400.

Augustus' settlement of 27 BC divided provinces into those governed by the emperor through legates (mostly the frontier provinces with legions) and the 'public' ones assigned by lot to senatorial proconsuls (Africa and Asia for ex-consuls, the rest for ex-praetors). Egypt was under an equestrian prefect. The terms 'senatorial' and 'imperial' are modern.

Judicial districts of a province, where the governor held assizes on a circuit (Asia had 13 by the early empire); also associations of Roman citizens resident in a provincial town (conventus civium Romanorum).
A self-governing community (city or tribe) with its territory (territorium), the basic unit of provincial administration and taxation; also citizenship (civitas Romana).

Self-governing community whose inhabitants held Roman citizenship (originally civitas sine suffragio) or Latin rights, with its own magistrates (duoviri or quattuorviri) and council; the Flavian municipal law from Spain (lex Irnitana) shows their charters.

Settlement of Roman or Latin citizens founded on conquered land: small citizen colonies guarding coasts (Ostia, Antium), large Latin colonies with independent status (Cales 334, Venusia 291, Aquileia 181), Gracchan and veteran colonies (Narbo 118; Caesar's and Augustus' foundations of perhaps 100 colonies). Later the title was a privileged rank granted to existing cities.

Status shared by members of the Latin league and later Latin colonies, with rights of trade (commercium) and intermarriage (conubium) with Romans and, for magistrates, Roman citizenship (from the later 2nd century). Extended to Transpadane Gaul (89 BC) and by Vespasian to all of Spain.
Roman citizenship without the vote, imposed on communities incorporated after the Latin War (338 BC), such as Capua and Caere, with obligations of military service and tax but internal autonomy.

The Italian communities bound to Rome by bilateral treaties, supplying troops (usually more than Rome's own legions) without paying tribute; their demand for citizenship produced the Social War (91-88 BC) and the enfranchisement of Italy south of the Po.

Formal treaty sworn with fetial rites: equal (aequum), like the Foedus Cassianum with the Latins (493 BC), or unequal, requiring the ally to respect the majesty of the Roman people. Late Roman foedera settled barbarian groups.

Unconditional surrender of a community into the power (in fidem or in dicionem) of the Roman people, after which Rome decided its fate; the Carthaginian deditio of 149 BC preceded the order to abandon the city.

glossary.term: friendship (amicitia) and 'friend of the Roman people'
glossary.def: Relationship of mutual goodwill between individuals or between Rome and kings and states (amicus et socius populi Romani), recorded on the Capitol, the basis of client-king relationships.

Dependent monarchy ruled by a 'friend and ally' of Rome (Numidia, Galatia, Cappadocia, Judaea, Mauretania, Thrace, Commagene, the Bosporus), offering frontier security and local knowledge; most were annexed in the 1st century AD, often on the ruler's death.

Late Roman administrative group of provinces under a vicarius, created under Diocletian (by c. 314 there were 12: Oriens, Pontica, Asiana, Thracia, Moesiae, Pannoniae, Italia, Africa, Hispaniae, Viennensis, Galliae, Britanniae). Later the church adopted the term for a bishop's see.

The largest late Roman administrative division, run by a praetorian prefect: by 395 Oriens, Illyricum, Italy-Africa and Gaul; Justinian added Africa (534). The prefecture handled taxation, the annona, supply, public works, the cursus publicus and appeals.
Governor of a diocese, deputy of the praetorian prefect, hearing appeals and supervising provincial governors; Justinian abolished several vicariates (535).

Common title of late Roman provincial governors (equestrian, later clarissimi), alongside consulares and correctores; civil only, since Diocletian and Constantine separated civil and military command.

'Companion' of the emperor: from Constantine a formal rank in three grades and a title for many offices: comes sacrarum largitionum (finance), comes rerum privatarum, comes domesticorum, comites rei militaris commanding regional armies, comites civitatum governing cities in the successor kingdoms (the origin of medieval counts).
Late Roman finance minister in charge of mints, mines, the precious-metal taxes (chrysargyron, aurum coronarium), state factories for luxury goods, and donatives to the army.
Late Roman commander of the troops (mainly limitanei) of a frontier region (dux limitis), often covering several provinces; ranked below the comites rei militaris. Origin of the medieval duke.

Supreme late Roman military commander, created by Constantine (magister peditum and magister equitum); later regional magistri (per Orientem, per Thracias, per Illyricum) and praesental magistri in the East. In the West the magister utriusque militiae (Stilicho, Constantius, Aetius, Ricimer, Gundobad, Orestes) dominated the emperor; in the East Leo I and Zeno broke the power of Aspar and the Isaurian generals.

'Master of the offices', a palatine minister created by Constantine controlling the secretariats (scrinia), the scholae, the agentes in rebus, the state arms factories, court ceremonial and reception of foreign embassies; John Lydus traces his rise at the expense of the prefects.
Late Roman chief legal minister who drafted imperial laws and replies to petitions; Tribonian held the office under Justinian.

Grand chamberlain, a eunuch heading the imperial bedchamber staff, often immensely influential (Eusebius under Constantius II, Eutropius under Arcadius, Chrysaphius under Theodosius II, Narses' early career).

Corps of imperial couriers and inspectors (successors of the frumentarii) under the magister officiorum, who carried messages, controlled the cursus publicus and served as heads of governors' staffs; widely feared as spies.
Imperial shorthand secretaries who kept records of the consistory and were sent on confidential missions; their chief was the primicerius notariorum (Joannes, usurper of 423, held the post).
The late Roman emperor's formal council, where members stood ('consistere') in the emperor's presence; included the chief palatine ministers.

An official register of offices and units, above all the Notitia Dignitatum (c. 395-420s), listing every senior office, its staff and insignia and the military units under each commander; also notitiae of provinces and bishoprics.

Late Roman official list of provinces or offices: the Verona List (c. 314), the Laterculus of Polemius Silvius (449) and Hierocles' Synekdemos (c. 527-528), the key evidence for provincial subdivision.
Greek title of the urban prefect of Constantinople (from 359), responsible for order, guilds, markets and the city's senate.

Governor combining civil and military authority over the remaining Byzantine territories of Italy (exarchate of Ravenna, attested from 584) and Africa (Carthage, from c. 591), created by Maurice to defend against Lombards and Moors. Heraclius' father was exarch of Africa and launched the revolt of 608-610 from there.

Honorific personal dignity created by Constantine for the highest officials; in the 5th-century West 'the patrician' became the title of the dominant generalissimo (Constantius, Aetius, Ricimer), and was granted to barbarian kings (Odoacer, Theodoric, later Clovis' successors).

The billeting system by which Roman landowners hosted soldiers; used to describe how barbarian federates were settled in Gaul and Italy (thirds of land or of tax revenue), a much-debated question (Goffart's tax-share theory vs land division).

The Blues and Greens (with lesser Reds and Whites), organizations that ran chariot racing and claques in the hippodromes of Constantinople and other cities; their riots culminated in the Nika revolt of 532 (some 30,000 killed) and played roles in the fall of Phocas (610).

Greek for general, used for Roman magistrates and commanders (strategos hypatos = consul) and in the 6th-7th centuries for army commanders; in the later themes the strategos combined military and civil authority. Precursors include the exarchs and Justinian's combined governors (e.g. the praetor of Thrace, 535).

Military-administrative districts of the middle Byzantine empire (Anatolikon, Armeniakon, Opsikion, Thrakesion), named after the field armies withdrawn to Anatolia after the Arab conquests of the 630s-640s. Older views (Ostrogorsky) credited Heraclius with creating the themes and soldiers' land-holdings; most scholars (Haldon, Kaegi) now see a gradual development from c. 640-660s, with civil and military powers merged under strategoi only later.
